snippet.title: How the most feared pirate of the history was killed? The cleverest trap in history.
snippet.description:
November 22, 1718. Ocracoke Inlet.

Lieutenant Maynard sailed in with a plan no pirate had ever seen — an empty deck, forty men hiding below, and the patience to take a broadside before springing the trap.

Blackbeard boarded what he thought was a broken ship. He found forty armed men waiting.

Five musket balls. Twenty sword wounds. He was still standing.

This is the true story of how the Golden Age of Piracy's most infamous captain met his end — not because he was outgunned, but because his own brilliance walked him into the one trap he couldn't read.

—
Sources: "A General Historie of the Pyrates" — Captain Charles Johnson (1724); Colonial records of the Battle of Ocracoke Inlet.

snippet.title: Henry Morgan: The Pirate Who Sacked a Spanish City | History for Sleep
snippet.description:
He was a pirate in all but name — and he did it with the blessing of a king. Henry Morgan led the buccaneers of the Caribbean on raids no one believed possible, marching his men through jungle and swamp to fall upon the richest cities of the Spanish empire. He plundered, he burned, and instead of the gallows, he was knighted and made a governor.

snippet.title: Recovering Queen Anne’s Revenge: Blackbeard’s Pirate Death Trap
snippet.description:
Queen Anne’s Revenge was Blackbeard’s most feared pirate flagship—but when it slammed into the deadly shallows of Beaufort Inlet, it became a buried trap of cannon, anchors, ballast, and secrets. Was this a simple navigational disaster, or did Blackbeard deliberately abandon the ship to escape with fewer men and more treasure?

This documentary follows the Queen Anne’s Revenge from its 1718 grounding to the modern recovery of one of the most important pirate shipwrecks ever found. Hidden beneath shifting North Carolina sand, the wreck was located through historical research, magnetometer survey, diver verification, and underwater archaeology. What investigators found was not a clean wooden hull, but a fused battlefield of iron: cannon, anchors, ballast stones, and ship hardware locked together by marine concretion.

The salvage challenge was extreme. Recovery teams could not simply rip the heavy iron from the seabed, because fragile hull timbers were trapped beneath the massive concretion pile. Every lift had to be planned like a dangerous puzzle. The recovery of Anchor A1 showed how careful heavy lift work could remove major artifacts without destroying the wreck’s hidden structure.

But the real battle began after recovery. Salt-filled iron from Queen Anne’s Revenge could destroy itself in open air, requiring wet storage, desalination, and electrolytic reduction. From pirate cannon to surviving paper fragments, this wreck reveals Blackbeard’s world through engineering, chemistry, and maritime history.

snippet.title: Japan's Most Feared Pirates Weren't Even Japanese
snippet.description:
For three hundred years, China and Korea feared the wokou, "Japanese pirates" who supposedly raided their coasts at will. The single most powerful pirate lord this so-called Japanese threat ever produced, the man whose private fleet could besiege Chinese county seats and threaten Nanjing, was a Chinese salt merchant's son named Wang Zhi who never set foot in Japan until he needed somewhere to base his smuggling empire. He's also the reason Portuguese matchlock guns reached Tanegashima in 1543 — guns that went on to reshape Sengoku-period warfare. We trace how a Ming trade ban manufactured a multi-ethnic piracy economy, why Chinese records put the real ethnic breakdown of "Japanese" raiders as mostly Chinese, how Wang Zhi built and lost an empire, and why a fragmented, ungoverned Japan was the real condition that let it all happen.
